title: Unicity through Complexity: EEG attractors at the OHBM BrainArt exhibition
subtitle: Two 1.5m canvases of resting brain activity, one neurotypical and one neuroatypical, and a question with no fair answer.
summary: My art project NeuropsyXart was selected for the 2023 Brain Art Exhibition at OHBM in Montréal: two large canvases, each one an eight-minute EEG attractor drawn as a single line — one from a neurotypical person, one from a neuroatypical person — with the viewer standing between them and asked which is which.
content: My art project, NeuropsyXart, was selected for the 2023 Brain Art Exhibition — the show the BrainArt Special Interest Group of the Organization for Human Brain Mapping puts on every year at the OHBM meeting, which in 2023 was in Montréal, 22–26 July. The theme was The Multifaceted Brain: Adaptation and Diversity, and the piece went in under the third of its three axes, Neurodiversity, in the written-text-or-still-image category. In July it went up on two easels on the exhibition floor (photograph).

The piece is two canvases, 1.5m by 1.5m, facing each other with just enough room between them for one person to stand. Each canvas is an EEG attractor: eight minutes of one person's brain activity, at rest, eyes closed, drawn as a single continuous line. One of them comes from a neurotypical person and the other from a neuroatypical person, and the only thing asked of whoever stands between them is which is which.

Neither canvas was composed, which is what makes that a fair question to put. What is on them is a property of the sitter's own physiology rather than of the artist, who is merely a facilitator, a tool; there is no authorship in there to read.

The usual way to draw brain activity is as a signal unfolding over time: a wiggly line, time along the bottom. An attractor plot — a state-space embedding, properly — drops time from the axes altogether and plots the signal against its own immediate past, so that every point is the state the system is in now against the state it was in a moment ago. The wiggle becomes a trajectory through a space of states rather than a history. Signals that look like noise in the first view often turn out, in the second, to be orbiting a well-defined region they never leave however long the recording runs: the boundaries of the system that produced them.

A screen between the easels carried an explanation of the method, which was the other half of the point. Aside from whatever the canvases are worth as art, the stand was a short introduction to what chaos theory is doing in neuroimaging — the family of indices (entropy, fractal dimension, and the rest) that we use in the lab's own work on complexity and that NeuroKit computes.
Many thanks to the BrainArt SIG for the invitation, the wall space and the easels. The rest of that year's exhibition is worth the detour — the full catalogue is online.
